The class visited a library near the station. Students chose books about places they hoped to visit and read a few pages in silence. One student found a map inside an old travel guide. Another compared two descriptions of the same city. The teacher asked everyone to explain one surprising detail to a partner. They then returned to the shelves to find evidence for their explanations. Before leaving, the group wrote questions that a later reading session could explore.
I explained the experience in a short message to a friend. Choosing specific examples made the account clearer and helped me remember details that I had almost forgotten.

Our school garden began with a narrow patch of soil beside the fence. At first the ground was dry and very few plants survived. We collected leaves, mixed them into the soil, and carried water from the playground tap. A neighbour showed us how to protect young roots without covering the stems. After several weeks small green shoots appeared. Students measured the plants on different mornings and recorded the weather. Their notes helped the next group decide where to plant beans.

On Saturday we walked along a river that crosses the town. Near the bridge the water moved quickly around stones and fallen branches. Farther downstream a broad pool reflected the trees. My friend noticed plastic bottles caught among the reeds, so we photographed the area and marked it on a map. We later joined residents who were cleaning the path. Listening to their memories showed us how the river had changed and why a familiar place deserves careful attention.

I learned to cook a vegetable soup with my grandmother. She placed the ingredients on the table and asked me to describe their colours and smells. While the onions softened, we talked about meals she remembered from childhood. I added the potatoes too early and had to change the cooking time. The soup still tasted good, although its texture was different from hers. Writing down what happened helped me understand that a recipe guides decisions but cannot replace observation.

Each label described how someone had used an object and why they had kept it. I spent several minutes looking at a repaired wooden chair. The visible repairs made its history easier to imagine. Our group discussed which ordinary possessions might tell future visitors something about our own lives, and we drafted labels for them.

We planned a short journey using buses rather than a car. The timetable looked simple until we noticed that some services ran only on weekdays. We compared several routes, allowed time to change buses, and chose an earlier departure. During the trip a driver suggested a quiet path beside a lake. The unexpected walk became the part we remembered best. Afterwards we compared the original plan with our experience and discussed which information would help another group make the journey.
